passages.happening:
Joab is told that the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom. ‘And that day’s victory was turned into mourning for all the people’ (verse 2). The troops creep back into the city as if they had lost the battle. The king covers his face and cries out at the top of his voice, “O my son Absalom! O Absalom, my son, my son!” (verse 4).

Joab goes in to the king. “Today you have disgraced all your servants who have saved your life” (verse 5), he says. “You love those who hate you and hate those who love you!” (verse 6). The king, he says, would have been pleased if Absalom were alive and all of them dead. Unless the king goes out and speaks kindly to his men, not one will stay with him that night (verse 7).

‘So the king got up and sat in the gate’ (verse 8), and all the people come before him.
passages.hearers:
Absalom is dead, and the kingdom is not yet healed. A victory celebration required the king to honor the men who had fought for him. Instead his mourning made them steal back into the city as though they had been beaten.

Joab is harsh, and he is the man who killed Absalom against the king's order. But his warning is real. The king's private grief is costing him his people. Sitting in the gate was where a king appeared to his people and heard their cases, so when David takes his seat there, he has taken up his role again.

The text does not rebuke David's grief, and it does not tell him to stop loving his son. It shows a man who must carry a father's sorrow and a king's duty at once.
passages.later: The Teacher in Ecclesiastes knew there was ‘a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance’ (Ecclesiastes 3:4). David had to find both on the same day.
passages.asks: Joab told David that his grief was costing him the people who loved him. Ask when private sorrow has to make room for others who need you. And ask who in your life is carrying a grief that no one has made room for.

passages.t: The way back, and Shimei spared
passages.happening:
All through the tribes of Israel the people argue. The king saved them from their enemies, and Absalom, whom they anointed, is dead, so why does no one speak of bringing the king back? David sends the priests Zadok and Abiathar to the elders of Judah, his own tribe, to ask why they should be the last to bring him home. He sends word to Amasa, Absalom's commander, that he will be commander of the army in place of Joab. ‘So he swayed the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man’ (verse 14), and they send for him.

The king comes back to the Jordan, and the men of Judah come to Gilgal to bring him across. Shimei, who had cursed him, hurries down with them, with a thousand men of Benjamin, and Ziba with his sons and servants. Shimei falls before the king and asks him not to hold his wrongdoing against him: ‘For your servant knows that I have sinned’ (verse 20).

Abishai asks whether Shimei should not die for cursing the LORD's anointed. And David replied, “Sons of Zeruiah, what have I to do with you, that you should be my adversaries today? Should any man be put to death in Israel today? Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?” (verse 22). So the king said to Shimei, “You shall not die” (verse 23), and he swears it.
passages.hearers:
David's kingdom joined two groups that had never fully merged. Judah made him king first at Hebron, and the northern tribes came seven years later. Both supported Absalom, and now each must decide whether to bring David back. David's strategy is political. He shames the elders of Judah into acting first, and he wins Absalom's followers by offering Absalom's commander the army. That move humiliates Joab, and the next chapter shows the result.

The verb to return runs through the chapter as the tribes debate bringing the king back. It is also the Old Testament's main word for repentance, turning back to God.

Gilgal, near Jericho, was a place of deep memory: Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan under Joshua, and the place where Saul's kingship was renewed. Crossing the Jordan at Gilgal made David's return a kind of second entry into the land.

Shimei's confession may be as much political as heartfelt, but it echoes David's own words to Nathan, and it gains him his life. David's question to Abishai sets the mood he wants for his return: no one is to die today. The word he uses for adversaries is satan, used here in its ordinary human sense of someone who stands in the way. David's mercy is real, and it is partial. Near his death he will ask Solomon to deal with Shimei.
passages.later:
Gilgal was where Israel first camped in the land: ‘the people went up from the Jordan and camped at Gilgal on the eastern border of Jericho’ (Joshua 4:19).

Shimei's pardon lasted David's lifetime. Solomon later bound him to stay in Jerusalem, and when he left the city, ‘Benaiah son of Jehoiada... went out and struck Shimei down’ (1 Kings 2:46).
passages.asks: David spared Shimei on the day of his return. Ask why mercy fits so well at a moment of new beginning. And ask whether there is someone you could release from a debt today, without pretending it was never owed.

passages.happening:
Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, comes down to meet the king. ‘He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king had left until the day he returned safely’ (verse 24).

The king asks him why he did not go with him. Mephibosheth answers that because he is lame, he had told his servant to saddle a donkey so that he could go with the king, but Ziba deceived him and slandered him to the king (verses 26-27). He leaves the matter in David's hands: the king is like the angel of God, so let him do what is good in his eyes. His whole family deserved death, he says, and yet the king set him among those who eat at his table (verses 27-28).

The king replied, “Why say any more? I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land” (verse 29). And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Mephibosheth's appearance tells its own story. Not caring for his feet, not trimming his mustache and not washing his clothes were signs of mourning, and he had kept them from the day David left. That supports his claim that he was loyal all along.

The woman of Tekoa had also said that the king was like the angel of God, wise enough to know all things (14:17, 20). Mephibosheth simply puts himself in the king's hands. Earlier, on one man's word, David gave Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth (16:4). Now he has heard both sides, and he divides the land.

What stands out is Mephibosheth's last sentence. Let Ziba take it all: the king's safe return matters more to him than his property, while many others in the chapter are bargaining for advantage.
passages.later: A proverb names the danger David fell into on the road out of the city: ‘He who answers a matter before he hears it’ (Proverbs 18:13) brings folly and disgrace on himself.
passages.hard:
Who was telling the truth, Ziba or Mephibosheth?

The text leaves this open, and readers disagree. Mephibosheth's appearance, unwashed and in mourning since David left, his explanation that Ziba took the donkeys and left him behind because he was lame, and his willingness to let Ziba take everything, all suggest that he was loyal and that Ziba lied to gain his master's land. Many interpreters conclude this.

Others point out that Mephibosheth, as Saul's heir, had reason to hope that the kingdom would return to his family, and that his words could be a clever defense. David's decision to divide the land has been read as a wise compromise, as a tired king avoiding a hard judgment, or as a failure of justice toward a loyal man. The narrator does not settle it.
passages.asks: Mephibosheth valued the king's return above his land. Ask what you are bargaining for that matters less than you think. And ask whether you have ever judged someone on one side of a story, and what you might do now that you have heard the other.

passages.t: Barzillai's farewell, and a quarrel over the king
passages.happening:
Barzillai the Gileadite, eighty years old and very wealthy, who had provided for the king at Mahanaim, comes down to see him across the Jordan. David invites him to come to Jerusalem and live at his side. Barzillai declines. He is too old to taste what he eats or to hear the singers; ‘Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother’ (verse 37). He offers Chimham, his son or relative, to go in his place. The king kisses Barzillai, ‘and blessed him’ (verse 39), and Barzillai goes home.

Then the quarrel begins. The men of Israel ask why the men of Judah took the king away for themselves. Judah answers that the king is their relative. “We have ten shares in the king,” answered the men of Israel, “so we have more claim to David than you” (verse 43). ‘But the men of Judah pressed even harder than the men of Israel’ (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
Barzillai's reply shows how old age was spoken of: taste and hearing gone, and the wish to die near the tomb of his parents. Burial in the family tomb mattered greatly. He is content to go home and let a younger man receive the king's reward.

The quarrel uses the picture of shares. Israel claims ten shares in the king, one for each of the northern tribes, while Judah claims to be his closer kin.

The chapter mirrors David's flight. Going out, he met Ziba, Shimei, Hushai and the men of Gilead. Coming back, he meets Shimei, Ziba, Mephibosheth and Barzillai. The verb to cross comes again and again as the Jordan becomes the stage for each meeting. The chapter began in grief and ends in quarreling, and neither is resolved. That fault line between Judah and the north leads straight to Sheba's revolt in the next chapter, and later it will split the kingdom in two.
passages.later: Barzillai's kindness was remembered. On his deathbed David told Solomon, ‘But show loving devotion to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite, and let them be among those who eat at your table’ (1 Kings 2:7). Centuries later a place near Bethlehem may still have carried Chimham's name: ‘Geruth Chimham, near Bethlehem’ (Jeremiah 41:17).
passages.asks: Barzillai was content to go home and let a younger man receive the reward. Ask what it would look like for you to be generous without needing to be repaid. And ask where you are arguing over who has the greater claim, when the thing itself is slipping away.
